# Content for people

Google's repeated message is to optimise for people: it asks for unique perspectives and expertise beyond common knowledge, says content made for Search will not succeed, and calls optimising for people optimising for generative AI Search. Day 2 tied this to indexing: Google said index selection aims to keep only documents useful now or later, that page quality ultimately decides indexing, and that 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is most often a quality issue rather than a technical one (the index-selection details were said at the event, not in Google's docs). Google repeated Day 1's advice to focus on users, saying that creating content users like is a better use of time than combing documentation for signals, and Google said both retrieval methods work from page content, so the content mantra of about 25 years still stands. Google's video talk added that paying for a generative AI subscription does not make AI-generated videos succeed. Day 3 made content quality central to ranking: Google's quality talk defined it, as the rater guidelines do, by effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy, contrasted commodity content built on common knowledge with unique, experienced takes, and said quality problems are quality issues, not AI versus human ones. Google added that pages need no synonym lists, because Google expands queries itself, and its guidance names writing to a word count or covering many topics in the hope of traffic as signs of search-engine-first content. Google's marketing research talk reached the same advice, optimise for people because a human makes the final decision, and the closing talk warned that chasing fan-out queries distracts from creating helpful content. A community case study, in which a niche article drew 28 times more clicks than a comprehensive one from far fewer impressions (no data source or period given), illustrated the point. A second recording of Day 1 added that the opening keynote closed with 'UEO', user engine optimisation, next to SEO and GEO: focus on the user and the rest will follow; it also said high-quality content may be created by humans or by AI, as long as it is made for users and not for search, and that information quality remains a core focus across Search, YouTube and Discover. Cherry Prommawin said quality is one of the most important things in ranking, and Gary Illyes said the natural content Google's algorithms understand and promote better includes content created, or at least edited and reviewed, by humans (said at the event). A Google host of the AI lightning talks advised always checking what AI tools do and focusing on what the business and its users need, and on Day 2 Gary Illyes said AI-generated images and videos must be checked for hallucinations. In Day 2's consolidation case study a community speaker kept only pages with real business potential, introduced the financial experts responsible for the content instead of an anonymous content factory, and credited the growth to quality rather than more content.

## What to do

- Prioritise unique expertise and first-hand experience over covering every possible need.
- Treat 'Crawled – currently not indexed' as a quality audit list: compare those URLs with indexed pages of the same type before hunting for technical faults.
- Put the terms a page should rank for in its main content and explain the topic fully in plain words, without keyword stuffing.
- Do not rewrite content into chunks or AI phrasing; write for readers.
- Judge every article, AI-assisted or not, by the effort, originality, skill and accuracy it adds beyond what an LLM would answer directly.
- Start content briefs from a concrete problem a real group of users has, and judge articles by clicks and conversions, not impressions.
- For reviews, test the products yourself and publish your own photos, measurements and test method.
- Show the real experts responsible for what the site publishes, especially on financial or other high-stakes topics.

  <br><sub>`D3-C121` · Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality (Community speakers)</sub>

- **[Stage]** The niche article in a community speaker's case study worked because the team stopped to analyse how people use the company's products and what the products bring them, then wrote about it.
  <br><sub>`D3-C124` · Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality (Community speakers)</sub>

- **[Stage]** A community speaker's exercise: step out of your shop, look at your site from across the street the way users do, and check what problems its pages solve.
  > "walk out of your shop. Stand on the other side of the street, look at the shop the way your users are looking at it"
  <br><sub>`D3-C128` · Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality (Community speakers)</sub>

- **[Stage]** If you cannot say what problems your pages solve for users, or the answer is 'it depends', you are optimising for the search engine rather than for people, and that will not work for long, a community speaker warned.
  <br><sub>`D3-C129` · Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality (Community speakers) · Repeats [D1-C013](../sessions/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk described quality as a ranking signal in its own right: a number calculated from many different parts (the word 'quality' is a repaired speech-to-text reading).
  <br><sub>`D3-C130` · Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality (Google) · not in Google docs</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said quality is one of the most important ranking signals, although Google uses hundreds of ranking signals (the word 'quality' is a repaired speech-to-text reading).
  <br><sub>`D3-C131` · Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Automatically generating and ranking results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/), [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide) · Extends [D3-C084](../sessions/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk defined content quality as the extent to which a human being put effort, originality, talent, skill and accuracy into creating the content.
  > "Quality is basically the extent to which a human being put effort, originality, talent, skill, and accuracy into creating content."
  <br><sub>`D3-C132` · Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf), [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) · Used by the glossary term *Content quality (effort, originality, talent or skill, accuracy)*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said quality is part of the core systems and signals that go into Google's algorithm, which Google calls ranking systems.
  <br><sub>`D3-C134` · Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide), [Automatically generating and ranking results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said Google designs its ranking systems to identify the information people are most likely to find useful and reliable.
  <br><sub>`D3-C148` · Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content), [Automatically generating and ranking results](https://www.google.com/search/howsearchworks/how-search-works/ranking-results/)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk showed five self-assessment questions (slide not photographed) that site owners can use to evaluate their own content, such as whether it is people-first or made mainly for search engines, and whether the author is an expert on the topic.
  <br><sub>`D3-C166` · Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality (Google) · consistent with Google docs · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk pointed to page 21 of the Search Quality Rater Guidelines for its definition of content quality by effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy, noting that the document is updated from time to time.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said effort, in the rater guidelines, is the extent to which a human being actively worked to create satisfying content, and that effort can be direct or indirect.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said originality means offering content that is not available on any other website or, where similar content exists elsewhere, adding more value to it.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said talent or skill means content created with enough talent and skill to give users a satisfying experience.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said content has to be accurate, and that accuracy matters most for YMYL topics and health topics.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk contrasted a commodity article, 'Top 10 things to consider when buying running shoes', with a non-commodity one, a wear pattern analysis of why certain running shoes collapse after 400 miles (slide not photographed).

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said commodity content is based on very common knowledge, could have been written by anyone and usually offers very little insight or additional value.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said non-commodity content offers a unique, experienced take, and advised writing content that readers will find very helpful and reliable.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said its article examples were illustrations, not a recipe: writing exactly that article is no guarantee that it will work.

- **[Stage]** Google's quality talk said the speaker believes content in any vertical can go very far when its creators invest in their own knowledge, effort and expertise.

- **[Slide]** Google's Discover slide defined E-E-A-T: experience means first-hand, personal experience with the topic, expertise the necessary knowledge or skill, and authoritativeness the extent to which the creator or website is known as a go-to source for the topic.

- **[Slide]** Google's Discover slide said trust comes first: untrustworthy pages have low E-E-A-T however experienced, expert or authoritative they seem.

  <br><sub>`D3-C223` · Day 3, Uncovering Trustworthy Experiences on Discover (Google) · confirmed by Google docs · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf), [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) · Used by the glossary term *E-E-A-T*</sub>

- **[Stage]** Answering the common question whether to fix individual pages or the whole site after a core update, Google advised taking a close look at the site as a whole and trying to be objective.

## What Google's documentation says

- **[Docs]** Google's guide says creating separate content for every variation of how people might search, including fan-out queries, primarily to manipulate rankings or AI responses violates its scaled content abuse policy. It adds that its AI systems can understand a page's relevance even without an exact match to the query.
  <br><sub>`D1-C129` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 1, How Search works and where's AI? · is the documentation · [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) · Extended by [D2-C741](../sessions/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) · Extended by [D3-C065](../sessions/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) · Extended by [D3-C212](../sessions/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) · Used by `DEV-AIF-03`, the glossary term *Scaled content abuse*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Search Central guide to Google Trends says to use Trends to inform a content strategy only where a topic fits the business and its users, and to focus on terms where the site has expertise and experience.
  > "you shouldn't write about something just because it's trending"
  <br><sub>`D2-C792` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 2, Google Trends · is the documentation · [Get started with Google Trends](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/monitor-debug/trends-start)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's SEO Starter Guide advises anticipating the different words readers search with (some search for 'charcuterie', others for 'cheese board') but not worrying about every variation, because Google's language matching systems relate pages to queries without the exact terms.
  <br><sub>`D3-C089` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · is the documentation · [Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's spam policies define keyword stuffing as filling a web page with keywords or numbers to manipulate rankings in Google Search, for example repeating the same words or phrases so often that it sounds unnatural.
  > "filling a web page with keywords or numbers in an attempt to manipulate rankings in Google Search results"
  <br><sub>`D3-C100` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · is the documentation · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to people-first content lists writing to a particular word count, in the belief that Google prefers one, as a warning sign of search engine-first content, and says Google has no preferred word count.
  > "Google has a preferred word count? (No, we don't.)"
  <br><sub>`D3-C101` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · is the documentation · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to people-first content lists producing lots of content on many different topics, in the hope that some of it performs well in search results, as a warning sign of search engine-first content.
  <br><sub>`D3-C103` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · is the documentation · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's ranking systems guide lists Panda as a retired system: announced in 2011 to better ensure that high-quality and original content appears in search results, it became part of the core ranking systems in 2015.
  <br><sub>`D3-C112` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · is the documentation · [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to people-first content says its automated ranking systems are designed to prioritise helpful, reliable information created to benefit people, not content created to manipulate search engine rankings.
  <br><sub>`D3-C117` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · is the documentation · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's ranking systems guide says the helpful content system, announced in 2022 as the Helpful Content Update to show original, helpful content written by people, for people, became part of the core ranking systems in March 2024.
  <br><sub>`D3-C118` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · is the documentation · [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's helpful-content guidance lists effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy as the main-content attributes search quality raters are trained to evaluate, and says using generative AI to produce large amounts of text without manual oversight or curation represents little to no effort.
  <br><sub>`D3-C176` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · is the documentation · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) · Used by `DEV-SPM-02`, the glossary term *Content quality (effort, originality, talent or skill, accuracy)*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide to optimizing for generative AI features contrasts commodity content, such as '7 Tips for First-Time Homebuyers', with non-commodity content that gives unique expert or experienced takes beyond common knowledge, such as a first-hand account of waiving a home inspection.
  <br><sub>`D3-C180` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · is the documentation · [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide) · Used by the glossary term *Commodity content*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's helpful-content guidance says product reviews build trust when readers understand how many products were tested, what the test results were and how the tests were conducted, with evidence of the work such as photographs.
  <br><sub>`D3-C195` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · is the documentation · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's Discover documentation says Discover uses many of the same signals and systems as Search to determine what is helpful, people-first content.
  <br><sub>`D3-C220` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Uncovering Trustworthy Experiences on Discover · is the documentation · [Discover and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-discover) · Used by the glossary term *Google Discover*</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether content presents information in a way that makes you want to trust it, such as clear sourcing, evidence of expertise and background about the author or the site, for example through an author page or the site's About page.
  <br><sub>`D3-C576` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Mastering the messy middle · is the documentation · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Docs]** Google's guide for generative AI features says creating content that people find unique, compelling and useful will likely influence a website's presence in generative AI search.
  <br><sub>`D3-C589` · Google Search Central · annotates Day 3, Mastering the messy middle · is the documentation · [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)</sub>

## Analysis

- **[Analysis]** Put the terms a page should rank for in its main content (title, headings, opening paragraphs) rather than only in sidebars, tag lists or footers; footer keyword blocks are unlikely to add ranking value.
  <br><sub>`D2-C317` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-HTM-02`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Do not rewrite pages into short, self-contained chunks for AI systems; Google says Gemini reads context windows of millions of tokens, so structure content for readers, with clear headings and complete explanations.
  <br><sub>`D2-C333` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Understanding what's on a page · Used by `DEV-AIF-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Treat 'Crawled – currently not indexed' as a quality audit list: compare those URLs with indexed pages of the same type for thin, duplicate or soft-404-like content and for template differences before looking for technical faults.
  <br><sub>`D2-C716` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, Deciding what goes in the index? · Extends [D1-C098](../sessions/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) · Used by `DEV-MON-03`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Write for both retrieval routes without keyword stuffing: name the page's subject in the plain words people search with, because posting lists match the words on the page, and explain the topic fully, because embedding retrieval matches meaning, so every keyword variation is unnecessary.
  <br><sub>`D2-C742` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 2, How does the index look like? · [Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide), [Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Write each page in the words its audience uses and drop synonym lists added for search engines: Google adds synonyms at query time, and blocks of keyword variants read as keyword stuffing, which Google's spam policies prohibit.
  <br><sub>`D3-C024` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries · Used by `DEV-INT-11`</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Before writing, search for each variant of a key term: if the variants bring up the same entity or near-identical results, use the term your audience uses; if one variant returns unrelated results, write that variant on the page.
  <br><sub>`D3-C047` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Making sense of users' queries</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Do not treat keyword-density or word-count scores from CMS plugins as editorial targets: Google's spam policies treat filling a page with keywords to manipulate rankings as keyword stuffing, and Google says it has no preferred word count.
  <br><sub>`D3-C099` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · [Spam policies for Google web search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies), [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Impressions and business value can diverge sharply, so judge each article by its clicks and conversions, not by its impressions alone, before deciding which content to expand or retire.
  <br><sub>`D3-C125` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For content planning, start briefs from a concrete problem a real group of users has with or around your product, such as a failing setup they need an alternative for, rather than from a broad keyword the page should rank for.
  <br><sub>`D3-C127` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Lightning session K: Facets of quality · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For content and development teams: plan improvements across content quality, internal links, page experience and freshness together; a project that pushes a single metric, such as keyword density or one link score, matches what Google said does not work.
  <br><sub>`D3-C144` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Use the rater guidelines as a description of what Google's ranking systems aim to reward, not as a checklist of ranking factors: rater scores evaluate Google's changes and are not used to rank any particular site.
  <br><sub>`D3-C169` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** The talk's originality test ('are you adding more value') matches Google's helpful-content question on content that draws on other sources, while the rater guidelines ask raters, where other websites have similar content, to consider whether the page is the original source; aim to be the original source, and add substantial value where you build on others.
  <br><sub>`D3-C173` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf), [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For editorial teams, the test for an AI-assisted article is the same as for any article: whether it adds effort, originality, skill and accuracy beyond what an LLM would answer directly; disclosure of AI use alone neither saves nor sinks a page.
  <br><sub>`D3-C191` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For content teams: turn reviews into non-commodity content by testing the products yourselves, publishing your own photos and measurements, explaining the test method and defining comparable metrics across products; a list of common buying tips is the commodity version.
  <br><sub>`D3-C196` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** On 1 October 2026, during the event, Google updated its generative AI content guide with rater-guideline material to keep its documentation in sync with its developer-event presentations, and the helpful-content page, updated the same day, carries the effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy definitions from the quality talk; cite those pages rather than the talk.
  <br><sub>`D3-C217` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, How Google thinks about Quality · [Latest documentation updates](https://developers.google.com/search/updates), [Google Search's guidance on using generative AI content on your website](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/using-gen-ai-content), [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** After a core update drop, plan a site-wide quality review instead of page-by-page fixes or a technical 'recovery': have someone outside the team assess the site, compare it with the pages that gained, and test whether users can finish their task, for example with short satisfaction surveys.
  <br><sub>`D3-C299` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, What are quality updates · [Google Search's core updates and your website](https://developers.google.com/search/updates/core-updates)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Content teams can feed the new Q&A attribute from real customer questions (support tickets, reviews, sales chats), answered factually per product; this is the detailed, merchant-owned data Google said AI shopping answers need.
  <br><sub>`D3-C411` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Shopping on Search: Beyond the blue links</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For content planning, read query groups (and their trending up and trending down views) as intent themes: write for the intent the group stands for, not for each spelling or phrasing variant in it.
  <br><sub>`D3-C427` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Inside Search Console: What’s New & How to Use It</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Google's ranking systems guide describes 'query deserves freshness' systems that show fresher content where it would be expected, which is narrower than a general preference for fresh content; refresh pages whose queries expect current information, and judge other refreshes by quality.
  <br><sub>`D3-C487` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Lightning session L: Understanding SERPs and your users · [A guide to Google Search ranking systems](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ranking-systems-guide) · Extends [D2-C656](../sessions/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md)</sub>

- **[Analysis]** For high-involvement products and services, make the double-check easy on your own site: company details, reviews, cancellation and return policies, guarantees and contact options should be on crawlable, indexable pages linked from product and service pages.
  <br><sub>`D3-C593` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Mastering the messy middle</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Content that helps AI-assisted shoppers names the few features that decide a category (for a phone, battery and camera), compares options on them and shows what similar buyers chose, which matches the ease, assistance and suggestion benefits Google described.
  <br><sub>`D3-C597` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Mastering the messy middle</sub>

- **[Analysis]** Show only real authors with real photos and verifiable profiles; never invent author personas or use AI-generated headshots, which Google's raters treat as deception.
  <br><sub>`D3-C693` · Ibrahim Anjro (author) · annotates Day 3, Wrapping all up: AI, Search, and making sense of everything. · [General Guidelines](https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/guidelines.raterhub.com/en//searchqualityevaluatorguidelines.pdf) · Used by `DEV-SPM-05`</sub>

## Built on these claims

The items of the developer and content kits that rest on this topic's claims.

- Requirement `DEV-AIF-02`: Spend no effort on llms.txt, AI text files or AI-specific markup for Google
- Requirement `DEV-AIF-03`: Structure content for readers instead of splitting it into small chunks for AI
- Requirement `DEV-HTM-02`: Place the words a page should rank for in its main content, not in footers or sidebars
- Requirement `DEV-IMG-08`: Keep the IPTC and C2PA metadata that marks AI-generated images
- Requirement `DEV-INT-11`: Write pages in the words, spellings and script the audience searches with, and never add synonym or variant lists
- Requirement `DEV-MON-03`: Watch the Page indexing report and treat its not-indexed reasons as a work list
- Requirement `DEV-SPM-02`: Do not generate large sets of low-value pages from templates, feeds or LLM output
- Requirement `DEV-SPM-05`: Publish AI-generated text, images and markup only after human review, and show only real authors
- Myth `M-002`: Cut your content into short, self-contained chunks so Google's AI can use it.
- Quote `Q-002`: Optimizing for people is optimizing for Generative AI Search
- Story angle `A-001`: Is SEO dead? Google's own answer from Barcelona
- Glossary term *Commodity content*
- Glossary term *Content quality (effort, originality, talent or skill, accuracy)*
- Glossary term *E-E-A-T*
- Glossary term *Google Discover*
- Glossary term *llms.txt*
- Glossary term *Scaled content abuse*
